items.stem: Define the term "sustainable yield".
items.answer: The rate of increase in natural capital that can be exploited without depleting the original stock or its potential for replenishment
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the rate of increase in natural capital that can be exploited without depleting the original stock or its potential for replenishment. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Families found in a stream survey (BMWP score after each family): Asellidae (water louse): 3; Heptageniidae (flat mayfly nymphs): 10; Leptoceridae (cased caddisfly larvae): 10; Gammaridae (freshwater shrimps): 6; Perlidae (stonefly nymphs): 10. (a) Calculate the BMWP score and the ASPT. (b) Interpret the result and explain why biotic indices complement chemical tests.
items.answer: (a) BMWP = 39; ASPT = 39/5 = 7.8 (b) good water quality (ASPT above about 5); high-scoring taxa (stoneflies, mayflies) need high dissolved oxygen, so their presence or absence integrates water quality over time, whereas a chemical test gives only a snapshot.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 39, A1 7.8. (b) R1 interpretation, R1 indicator species reflect conditions over time / pollution-sensitive taxa.

items.stem: A student group used capture-mark-release-recapture on grasshoppers in an unmown meadow: first sample 83 (all marked with a spot of correction fluid on the thorax); second sample 64, including 15 marked animals. (a) Estimate the population size using the Lincoln index. (b) State two assumptions of the method.
items.answer: (a) 83 × 64 / 15 ≈ 354 (b) e.g. marks are not lost and do not affect survival or behaviour; marked individuals mix fully with the population; no births, deaths or migration between samples; equal chance of capture.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 substitution, A1 ≈ 354. (b) [1] each for two valid assumptions.

items.stem: A systems diagram of a reservoir behind a hydroelectric dam shows a storage of 214 million m³, an input (river inflow) of 65 million m³ per year and an output (outflow through turbines and evaporation) of 57 million m³ per year. Calculate the storage after one year.
items.answer: ΔS = inputs − outputs = 65 − 57 = +8 million m³; storage = 222 million m³; not in steady state (inputs ≠ outputs)
items.markingKey: M1 inputs − outputs; A1 +8 (storage 222).

items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "Protecting upwelling ecosystems is essential for global food security."
items.answer: Upwelling ecosystems are disproportionately important for fisheries and should be protected, though they are only one part of food security.

items.stem: Outline how high biodiversity increases the resilience of an ecosystem.
items.answer: More species means more feeding pathways and functional redundancy, so if one species declines another can fill its role; genetic diversity allows adaptation to change.
items.markingKey: More species means more feeding pathways and functional redundancy, so if one species declines another can fill its role; genetic diversity allows adaptation to change. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Outline why island species are particularly vulnerable to human impacts.
items.answer: Small ranges and populations, high endemism, and evolution without predators (e.g. flightless birds) mean introduced predators and habitat loss quickly cause extinction.
items.markingKey: Small ranges and populations, high endemism, and evolution without predators (e.g. flightless birds) mean introduced predators and habitat loss quickly cause extinction. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: State two differences between interspecific competition and intraspecific competition.
items.answer: Interspecific competition is between different species (e.g. red and grey squirrels); intraspecific competition is within one species (e.g. barnacles competing for rock space).
items.markingKey: Interspecific competition is between different species (e.g. red and grey squirrels); intraspecific competition is within one species (e.g. barnacles competing for rock space). [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: Water-balance data for a small catchment in the Scottish Highlands (area 85 km²): precipitation 650 mm; evapotranspiration 220 mm; change in storage +40 mm. (a) Calculate annual runoff in mm. (b) Convert this to a volume in million m³. (c) Predict and explain how deforestation of the catchment would change E, Q and flood risk.
items.answer: (a) 390 mm (b) 390 mm = 0.39 m over 85 × 10⁶ m² = 33.1 million m³ (c) less interception and transpiration → E falls; infiltration falls as soils compact → overland flow and Q rise; shorter lag time and higher peak discharge increase flood risk.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 390. (b) M1 depth × area, A1 33.1. (c) R1 E falls, R1 Q/overland flow rises, R1 flood risk with reason.

items.stem: Outline why photosynthesis and respiration are both examples of transformations.
items.answer: Photosynthesis transforms light energy into chemical energy and inorganic CO₂ and water into organic glucose; respiration transforms chemical energy into usable energy (ATP) and heat, and organic matter back to CO₂ and water.
items.markingKey: Photosynthesis transforms light energy into chemical energy and inorganic CO₂ and water into organic glucose; respiration transforms chemical energy into usable energy (ATP) and heat, and organic matter back to CO₂ and water. [1] per valid point, up to [4].

items.stem: Explain nutrient limitation of marine productivity, referring in detail to the Peruvian upwelling and to at least one other example you have studied. [7]
items.answer: Cold, nutrient-rich water rising off Peru supports some of the world's highest marine productivity and the anchoveta fishery (up to about 10 million t a year). Upwelling brings nitrates and phosphates to the sunlit surface, removing the nutrient limitation found in most of the open ocean. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem: Explain carrying capacity and the risks of removing predators, referring in detail to the Kaibab Plateau deer, Arizona and to at least one other example you have studied. [7]

items.stem: A river draining into the Baltic Sea has a nitrate concentration of 2.7 mg/L and a mean discharge of 10.3 m³/s. (1 mg/L = 1 g/m³; there are 86,400 s in a day.) (a) Calculate the daily nitrate load in kg. (b) Calculate the load if catchment measures cut the concentration by 50%. (c) Explain how this nitrate could cause eutrophication downstream and suggest two measures to achieve the reduction.
items.answer: (a) 2.7 g/m³ × 10.3 m³/s × 86,400 s = 2,403 kg per day (b) 1,201 kg per day (c) nitrate fertilises algal growth → algal bloom shades out plants → algae die and are decomposed by bacteria → BOD rises and DO falls → fish die (hypoxic "dead zone"). Measures: buffer strips and wetlands, precision fertiliser application / nitrate vulnerable zones, cover crops, upgrading sewage treatment.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 concentration × discharge × time, A1 2,403. (b) A1. (c) R1 R1 eutrophication sequence, R1 two measures.

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Data (study of the Brazilian Amazon, 2000-2012): mean annual deforestation rate inside Indigenous territories 0.15%; in strictly protected areas 0.40%; on unprotected land 2.0%.

Calculate how many times higher deforestation was on unprotected land than in Indigenous territories, and suggest one reason for the difference.
items.answer: 2.0 / 0.15 ≈ 13 times; Indigenous peoples actively defend territories and have customary rules limiting clearance; legal tenure blocks ranching expansion.
items.markingKey: 2.0 / 0.15 ≈ 13 times; Indigenous peoples actively defend territories and have customary rules limiting clearance; legal tenure blocks ranching expansion. Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: A Schaefer surplus-production model for southern bluefin tuna gives intrinsic growth rate r = 0.4 per year and carrying capacity K = 1,000 thousand tonnes; surplus yield Y = rN(1 − N/K). The stock is currently estimated at 800 thousand tonnes. (a) Calculate the MSY and the current surplus yield. (b) A fishing industry body proposes a quota of 110 thousand tonnes per year. Explain the likely consequence for the stock. (c) Evaluate the use of MSY as the basis of fisheries management, with reference to a named fishery.
items.answer: (a) MSY = 100 thousand tonnes per year at N = 500; current Y = 0.4 × 800 × (1 − 800/1000) = 64.0 thousand tonnes per year (b) the quota exceeds both MSY and current surplus production, so the catch removes more than natural increase; the stock will decline, reducing future yields and risking collapse (as with Grand Banks cod, 1992). (c) MSY gives a clear, science-based target, but r and K are uncertain and change with environment; it ignores age structure, bycatch and ecosystem interactions; variable recruitment and political pressure lead to quotas above advice; precautionary targets (e.g. F below F_MSY, ecosystem-based management) are safer.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 100, M1 substitution, A1 64.0. (b) R1 harvest > surplus → decline, R1 named consequence. (c) R1 strength, R1 limitation with example.

items.stem: Outline how deforestation can change the hydrological cycle of a region.
items.answer: Less interception and transpiration reduce atmospheric moisture and local rainfall; more runoff and soil erosion; faster flood peaks; in the Amazon, about a third to half of rainfall is recycled by forest transpiration.

items.stem: Outline why chemical tests and biotic indices should be used together.
items.answer: Chemical tests give precise values of specific pollutants at one moment but can miss intermittent discharges; biotic indices integrate conditions over time but do not identify the pollutant; together they give a fuller picture.
items.markingKey: Chemical tests give precise values of specific pollutants at one moment but can miss intermittent discharges; biotic indices integrate conditions over time but do not identify the pollutant; together they give a fuller picture. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Country A has 5 million people, an ecological footprint of 5.5 gha per person and a biocapacity of 0.7 gha per person. Global biocapacity is about 1.6 gha per person. (a) Calculate the national ecological deficit in gha. (b) Calculate how many Earths would be needed if everyone lived like the average resident. (c) Explain two ways a country can sustain a footprint larger than its biocapacity.
items.answer: (a) |5.5 − 0.7| × 5 million = 24.0 million gha (deficit) (b) 5.5 / 1.6 ≈ 3.4 Earths (c) importing food, timber and other resources (using other countries' biocapacity); emitting CO₂ absorbed by the global commons (oceans, forests elsewhere); running down its own natural capital (overfishing, deforestation).
items.markingKey: (a) A1 24.0 million gha. (b) A1 3.4. (c) R1 R1 trade / global commons / depletion.

items.stem: Outline how climate change contributes to biodiversity loss.
items.answer: Species ranges shift faster than many can move, phenology becomes mismatched (e.g. caterpillar peak and bird breeding), coral bleaching, and extreme events and droughts increase mortality.
items.markingKey: Species ranges shift faster than many can move, phenology becomes mismatched (e.g. caterpillar peak and bird breeding), coral bleaching, and extreme events and droughts increase mortality. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: State two differences between tropical rainforest and temperate deciduous forest.
items.answer: Tropical rainforests are hot and wet all year with very high diversity, many layers and rapid nutrient cycling; temperate deciduous forests have seasonal temperatures, trees that shed leaves in winter, lower diversity and richer soils with slower decomposition.
items.markingKey: Tropical rainforests are hot and wet all year with very high diversity, many layers and rapid nutrient cycling; temperate deciduous forests have seasonal temperatures, trees that shed leaves in winter, lower diversity and richer soils with slower decomposition. items.stem: Outline why mangrove loss is a significant source of carbon emissions.
items.answer: Mangroves store large amounts of carbon in waterlogged sediments; clearing for shrimp farms exposes sediments to oxygen, releasing stored carbon, and removes future sequestration.

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Data: Peruvian anchoveta landings (million tonnes, approximate) - 1970: 12.3; 1972: 4.7; 1973: 1.7; 1983 (El Niño year): 0.1; 1994: 9.8; 1998 (El Niño year): 1.2.

Explain why landings fell sharply in El Niño years.
items.answer: Weaker trade winds reduce upwelling; warm, nutrient-poor water lowers phytoplankton productivity; anchoveta move deeper or south or die, so catches fall.

items.stem: Outline why transboundary rivers can lead to conflict.
items.answer: Upstream countries can dam or divert water, reducing flow, quality and sediment downstream; demand is rising with population and irrigation; treaties may be outdated or exclude some states (e.g. 1959 Nile Agreement excluded Ethiopia).

items.stem: With reference to the giant panda, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in a successful downgrading of conservation status. [7]

items.stem: With reference to the Studland sand-dune system, Dorset, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in zonation linked to succession on dunes. [7]
items.answer: Transects show embryo dunes with sea couch, yellow dunes dominated by marram, grey dunes with lichens and heath further inland. items.stem: "The ecological footprint is the best measure of a country's environmental sustainability." Discuss this statement with reference to named examples. [9]
items.answer: It is a useful headline indicator but must be combined with others (water footprint, planetary boundaries, HDI) for a full picture.
